text: A paraglider is a soft fabric wing with no engine. In still air, it always sinks slowly, like a [[@how-paper-airplane-best|paper plane]]. Pilots stay up by finding air that rises faster than they sink.

The main sources are thermals, columns of warm air rising from sun-heated ground, and ridge lift, where wind hits a hill and is pushed upwards. Ride a strong thermal and you can climb hundreds of metres in minutes. Glide to the next one, climb again, and keep going. Good pilots stay up for hours and travel hundreds of kilometres in a day.

st.prompt: A paraglider pilot sees a hawk circling tightly without flapping. What should the pilot do?

options.t: Fly over and circle under it, because the hawk is riding rising air
Fly away fast, because hawks attack gliders
Land at once, because a storm is coming

st.reveal: Birds such as hawks, eagles and vultures find thermals by feel. When a bird circles without flapping, it is usually climbing in a column of warm, rising air, so pilots often join it.

d.try: See warm air rise. With an adult, hold a tissue strip or a light feather a little above a radiator, a sunny window sill or a mug of hot water (not touching it). Watch it lift and flutter. That rising air is a tiny thermal, the same kind of lift a paraglider rides.
myth: A paraglider is just a parachute that floats slowly down.
A parachute is built to fall slowly. A paraglider is a true wing. It moves forward and creates lift, so a pilot can steer, glide for many kilometres and even climb thousands of metres in rising air.

sec.t:
A paraglider wing is made of thin, strong nylon, often about 25 m² in area, roughly the size of a small room. It weighs only about 4 to 6 kg and can be folded into a backpack.

The wing is made of many tubes called cells, open at the front. As the pilot runs down a slope, air rushes into the cells and inflates the wing into a firm, curved shape. Hundreds of thin lines connect it to the pilot's harness. The curved top makes air flow faster over the wing than under it, which creates [[lift|lift]], just like on an aeroplane.

When the Sun heats the ground, some patches warm faster than others: ploughed fields, rocky slopes, car parks. Air above them warms, gets lighter and rises in a bubble or column.

Pilots can't see thermals, so they look for clues. A puffy cumulus cloud often forms at the top of one. Dust swirls, rising leaves and circling birds give it away too. [[@vultures-india|Vultures]] are experts. They can soar all day hardly flapping their wings, and pilots often share thermals with them.

A small device called a variometer beeps faster as the pilot climbs. The pilot then circles tightly to stay inside the rising air.

On windy days, pilots fly along hills and cliffs. Wind blowing against the slope gets pushed up, and the glider rides that rising air like a surfer on a wave, sometimes for hours.

The longest flights happen over flat, hot land with strong, steady thermals and wind behind the pilot. In northeast Brazil and in Texas, pilots have covered more than 550 km in one day. That is farther than a straight line from Bengaluru to Hyderabad.

India has some excellent flying sites. At Bir Billing in [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], pilots launch from a meadow at about 2,400 m and land in Bir, about 1,000 m lower. The site hosted the Paragliding World Cup in 2015. Kamshet near Pune and the hills of Sikkim are popular too.

Many visitors try tandem flights, sitting in front of a trained pilot on a double harness.

Thermals can also turn dangerous. Under a big thundercloud, the air rises so fast that a glider can be sucked up. In 2007, a German pilot, Ewa Wiśniewska, was pulled to nearly 10,000 m during a competition in Australia. She passed out in the freezing, thin air and woke up covered in ice, still flying. She survived and landed safely.

That is why pilots study the weather before every flight and avoid towering storm clouds. Learning to read the sky is half of flying, and the shapes of [[@clouds-types|clouds]] tell pilots more than any weather app.

text: India has a long coastline, more than 7,500 km by the older official measurement and about 11,000 km by a newer one that counts every bend. Along it live millions of people whose families have fished for generations. Before radios and phones, they learned to read the sea with their senses. A change in the colour of the water could point to fish. So could a flock of seabirds diving into the waves. A shift in the wind or a line of clouds on the horizon could warn that a storm was coming.

That knowledge was passed down by watching, listening and doing. Today, [[@people-fishing-villages|many fishers]] combine it with [[@satellites-help|satellite]] forecasts and mobile phones. The sea is the same, but the tools have changed.

st.prompt: Why does India stop most fishing from its coasts for about two months every year?

options.t: Many fish breed then, and the monsoon makes the sea dangerous
The fish swim too deep to catch in summer
Fishing boats are needed to carry rice

st.reveal: On the west coast, the ban runs through June and July, during the stormy monsoon and the breeding season of many fish. On the east coast it falls from mid-April to mid-June. The break keeps boats safe and gives fish time to breed.

d.try: Keep a sky and sea diary for a week, even if you live far from the coast. Each morning, note the wind (calm, breezy or strong), the clouds and any birds you see. Check a weather forecast and see if your notes helped you guess what was coming. That is how sea-reading begins.
myth: Catamarans were invented in the West as modern racing boats.

The word comes from the Tamil "kattumaram", a raft of logs tied together, used by fishers on India's east coast for centuries. English sailors borrowed the word, and it later came to mean any boat with two hulls.

sec.h: Signs in the water and sky
sec.t:
Experienced fishers notice details that others miss. Seabirds diving in one spot often mean a shoal of small fish just below. A patch of water with a different colour or texture can mean fish are gathering. Dolphins chasing fish near the surface are another clue.

The sky matters too. Wind direction, the shape of clouds and the swell rolling in from far away all hint at the coming weather. Waves made by a distant storm can arrive before the storm itself, as you can read in [[@waves-how|how waves form]]. Fishers also plan around the [[@tides|tides]] and the phases of the Moon, which change how fish move along the shore.

The [[@monsoon|monsoon]] shapes the fishing calendar. From June, strong winds and high waves make the Arabian Sea dangerous for small boats. Many fish also breed at this time. So the government bans most mechanised fishing for 61 days. On the west coast the ban runs through June and July. On the east coast, where the stormy season comes at a different time, it runs from mid-April to mid-June.

During the break, families mend nets, repair boats and wait for the sea to calm. When fishing restarts, there are often big catches. [[cyclone|Cyclones]] are still a serious danger, which is why fishers now listen carefully to weather warnings broadcast on radio and sent to phones.

Technology has added new ways of reading the sea. INCOIS, a government centre in Hyderabad, uses [[@satellites-india|satellites]] to measure the temperature and colour of the sea's surface. Where cooler, greener water rich in [[plankton|plankton]] meets warmer water, fish often gather. INCOIS sends maps of these likely fishing zones to fishers in many languages.

[[@mobile-networks|Mobile phones]] changed fishing in [[@kerala|Kerala]] too. A well-known study found that once fishers could call markets from their boats, they sold their catch where prices were best, and less fish [[@food-waste|went to waste]]. In 2018, during terrible [[@floods-why|floods]], Kerala's fishers brought their boats inland and rescued thousands of people. Their knowledge of water saved lives far from the sea.

text: Most animals are born, grow up, grow old and die. One small jellyfish, *Turritopsis dohrnii*, can skip the last part. When it is hurt, starving or stressed, it can turn its adult body back into its baby form and grow up all over again.
Scientists call it biologically immortal. That doesn't mean it can never die. It can still be eaten by a fish or killed by disease, and most of them are. But it doesn't have to die of old age.

Jellyfish in general are survivors. They have no brain, no heart and [[@what-if-no-bones|no bones]], and their bodies are about 95% water. Yet they have been drifting through the oceans for more than 500 million years.

st.prompt: Can any animal turn itself young again?

options.t: No, that's impossible
Yes, one jellyfish can

st.reveal: Yes! When it's injured or stressed, the ‘immortal jellyfish’ Turritopsis can turn back into a polyp, its baby stage, and grow up all over again. It can still be eaten or get sick, though.
st.nudge: It sounds impossible! But one tiny jellyfish does something like it.

src: Piraino S. et al. (1996) Reversing the life cycle: medusae transforming into polyps. Biological Bulletin 190.

d.try: Fill a bucket with water and drop in a clear plastic bag. Watch it drift and billow. From above it almost disappears, and it looks a lot like a jellyfish. That is why sea turtles, which love to eat jellyfish, sometimes swallow plastic bags by mistake.
myth: Peeing on a jellyfish sting makes it better.
It doesn't help and can make the sting worse. Lifeguards usually rinse a sting with seawater and remove any tentacles carefully, and a bad sting needs a doctor.

sec.t:
Most jellyfish live two very different lives. They start as a tiny [[polyp|polyp]] stuck to a rock, like a little flower on a stalk. The polyp buds off baby jellyfish, which swim away and grow into the floating bell shape we know, called a medusa.

Normally, a medusa lays eggs and dies. *Turritopsis* can run the film backwards. Its bell shrinks into a blob, sinks, sticks to the seabed and becomes a polyp again. That polyp then buds off fresh young jellyfish, with the same [[gene|genes]] as the old one.

In 1988 a German student called Christian Sommer was keeping these jellyfish in dishes in Italy. He noticed that they kept disappearing and polyps kept appearing in their place. A few years later, scientists confirmed what was happening.

Instead of a brain, a jellyfish has a net of nerves spread through its body. It still manages to swim, hunt and dodge danger. Box jellyfish have 24 eyes, arranged in four clusters around the bell. Some of those eyes can form rough pictures.

The tentacles carry thousands of stinging cells. Each one holds a coiled thread with a tiny harpoon. When something brushes it, the harpoon fires out in less than a millionth of a second, one of the fastest movements in nature. [[@jellyfish-sting|Most stings]] feel like a nettle. A few, like those of some Australian box jellyfish, can be very dangerous.

In 1991, the US space shuttle Columbia carried more than 2,000 moon jellyfish polyps into [[orbit|orbit]]. In space they multiplied into tens of thousands of baby jellyfish. Back on Earth, some of the space-born jellies had trouble telling which way was down. Jellyfish sense [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] with tiny crystals, and in space those crystals had nothing to fall towards. Astronauts' bodies face a similar puzzle, which you can explore in [[@space-body|space and the body]].

Today, jellyfish numbers seem to be rising in some seas, perhaps helped by warmer water and [[@fishing-sustainable|overfishing]]. Huge swarms have clogged fishing nets in Japan and blocked the water pipes of power stations. [[@sea-turtles|Sea turtles]] help keep them in check. A big leatherback turtle can gulp down hundreds of kilograms of jellyfish in a day, which is a lot of jelly for very little food.

text: A port is where the sea meets the land, and its whole job is moving cargo between the two as quickly as possible. A giant ship arrives, a harbour pilot guides it in, and tugboats nudge it against the dock. Then enormous cranes lift steel containers off the ship and onto trucks or trains, and load new ones back on.

Ports have deep channels so ships don't scrape the bottom, long quays where ships can tie up, and huge yards where containers are stacked like building blocks. They also have customs officers who check what comes in, since almost everything you own may have spent part of its life on a ship.

st.prompt: A giant ship is entering a busy harbour. Who usually steers it into port?

The captain alone, using GPS

st.reveal: Most big ports require a harbour pilot, an expert in the local channels, tides and currents, to come aboard and guide the ship in. The pilot often climbs up a rope ladder from a small boat while both are moving. Tugboats then help push and pull the ship against the dock.

myth: Big ships steer themselves into port, just like they sail across the ocean.
Ships are hard to steer at low speed and can take kilometres to stop. In narrow harbours, local pilots and tugboats guide them in, because one mistake could block a channel or damage a dock.

sec.h: The box that changed the world
sec.t:
For thousands of years, ships were loaded by hand. Workers carried sacks, barrels and crates up gangplanks, one at a time. A big ship could sit in port for a week or more, and goods were often lost or stolen.

In 1956, an American trucking businessman named Malcolm McLean sent a converted tanker called the Ideal X from Newark to Houston carrying 58 metal boxes. Each could be lifted straight off a truck and onto the ship. Soon containers came in standard sizes, 20 or 40 feet long, so the same box could ride a ship, a train and a truck without being opened. Loading costs dropped sharply, and [[@trade-world|world trade]] grew fast.

People have built harbours for thousands of years. At Lothal in Gujarat, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found a large brick basin over 4,000 years old. Many think it was a dockyard where Harappan boats loaded goods, which would make it one of the oldest known docks anywhere. Others suggest it was a [[reservoir|reservoir]]. Either way, the [[@harappan-trade|Harappans traded]] by sea with lands as far as Mesopotamia.

Today, Shanghai in China is the world's busiest container port. In the United States, the side-by-side ports of [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]] and Long Beach handle a large share of goods arriving from Asia. In India, big ports include Jawaharlal Nehru Port near Mumbai and Mundra in Gujarat. In 2024, a new deep-water port at Vizhinjam in Kerala began receiving huge container ships, close to one of the world's busiest shipping routes.

Ports are so connected that trouble in one spot can ripple around the world. In 2021, a giant container ship called the Ever Given got stuck across [[@suez-canal|the Suez Canal]] in Egypt. For six days, hundreds of ships waited at either end, and deliveries of everything from furniture to car parts were delayed for weeks.

That is why port workers, pilots and planners work around the clock. A port that runs smoothly is invisible to most people. A port that stops can empty shop shelves on the other side of the planet.

text: Ants work together by following simple rules and talking with smells. Each ant reacts to what is right around it: the scent of a trail, the touch of another ant, a crumb of food. No ant sees the big picture, and no ant gives orders.

But when thousands of ants follow the same simple rules, the colony as a whole acts cleverly. It finds the shortest path to food, builds nests with tunnels and chambers, and sends more workers wherever they're needed. Scientists sometimes call a colony a superorganism, because it behaves almost like one big animal made of many small bodies.

st.prompt: In an ant colony, who decides where the workers go to look for food?

options.t: Nobody. Ants follow scent trails left by other ants
The queen gives the orders
The oldest worker leads the way

st.reveal: A worker that finds food lays a scent trail on the way home. Others follow it and add more scent if they find food too. Good trails get stronger, and poor ones fade away, so the colony "decides" without a leader.

d.try: On a balcony or in a garden, with an adult nearby, put a tiny pinch of sugar on one piece of paper and a pinch of salt on another, a little way from an ant trail. Check every ten minutes. Then gently wipe your finger across the trail and watch what the ants do when the scent is broken.
myth: The queen ant rules the colony and tells the other ants what to do.

The queen is the colony's mother, not its boss. She lays the eggs. The work of building, foraging and defending is organised by thousands of workers following simple rules and reacting to smells and touch.
facts: Indian weaver ants build nests by stitching leaves with silk from their larvae

sec.t:
Ants communicate mostly with chemicals called [[pheromone|pheromones]]. They give off different ones for different messages. One means "food this way". Another means "danger, come and help". Ants also recognise their nestmates by smell, so a stranger from another colony is spotted instantly.

When a worker finds food, it heads home laying a trail of scent with the tip of its body. Other ants pick up the scent with their antennae and follow it. If they find food, they add their own scent on the way back. A good food source quickly gets a strong trail with hundreds of ants. When the food runs out, ants stop topping up the scent, and the trail fades within minutes.

Most ants in a colony are female workers. Young workers often stay inside, caring for eggs and [[larva|larvae]]. Older ones go outside to forage and defend, which is riskier. In some [[species|species]], workers come in different sizes. Big-headed soldiers guard the nest, and tiny ones tend the young.

The queen's main job is laying eggs, sometimes for many years. Male ants live only a short time. Their role is to mate with new queens, which then fly off to start colonies of their own.

In India and southeast Asia, weaver ants make nests high in mango and other trees. Workers form a living chain, gripping each other's waists, to pull two leaves together. Then other workers hold larvae against the leaf edges. The larvae give out silk, and the ants use them like tubes of glue to stitch the leaves shut. Some people in eastern India eat these ants as a spicy [[@insects-food|chutney]].

In the Americas, leafcutter ants carry pieces of leaves underground. They don't eat the leaves. They chew them up to grow a [[fungus|fungus]], which they then eat, much like farmers growing a crop. [[@termite-mounds|Termites]] in Africa and Asia farm fungus too, though they are not close relatives of ants.

Army ants in Central and South America have no fixed nest. When they reach a gap, some workers link their bodies to [[@power-ant-bridges|make a bridge]] for the others to cross. Fire ants, during floods, grip each other to form a floating raft with the queen safe in the middle.

There are so many ants that their total weight is thought to be greater than that of all wild birds and wild [[mammal|mammals]] put together. They turn soil, spread seeds and clean up dead insects. Look under any stone in a garden and you're likely to find a colony at work.

text: Bharatanatyam tells stories through *abhinaya*, the art of expression. A dancer acts out the words of a song with her face, eyes and hands, while her feet keep a precise [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]]. One dancer can play every character, switching from a god to a demon to a worried mother in a heartbeat.

The dance comes from Tamil Nadu in southern India. It is famous for its sharp lines and its half-sitting position, called *araimandi*, with knees bent out to the sides. A live group of musicians plays [[@carnatic-hindustani|Carnatic music]] as the dancer performs, often for an hour or more.

st.prompt: In Bharatanatyam, a single dancer often tells a story with several characters. How?

options.t: By switching between characters using face, posture and hand gestures
By changing costumes behind a curtain
By having a narrator act it out first

st.reveal: A dancer can turn from a fierce king into a frightened deer in a second, just by changing posture, eyes and hands. The audience follows the song's words and the dancer's face.

d.try: Choose a short story you know well, such as a crow dropping pebbles into a pot. Act it out without words, using only your face and hands. Play the crow, then the pot, then the water. Ask a friend to guess each character as you switch.
myth: Bharatanatyam has always been called by that name.
For a long time, the dance was called sadir or dasi attam. The name Bharatanatyam, linking it to the ancient sage Bharata, became popular in the 1930s.
facts: araimandi, a half-sitting position with knees bent outwards

sec.t:
A Bharatanatyam concert usually follows a set order called the *margam*. This order was shaped in the early 1800s by four brothers known as the Thanjavur Quartet, musicians at the court of the [[@marathas|Maratha king]] of Thanjavur.

It begins with *alarippu*, a short warm-up that wakes up the eyes, neck, arms and feet. Pure dance pieces follow. The centrepiece is the *varnam*, often the longest item, mixing fast footwork with long passages of storytelling. Slower pieces called *padams* are mostly acting. The concert ends with the *tillana*, a bright burst of [[rhythm|rhythm]].

sec.h: Telling a story with no words
sec.t:
Here is how a dancer might show a single line about the god [[@myths-krishna-childhood|Krishna stealing butter]]. Her hands become a pot. Her eyes dart left and right, checking that nobody is watching. She dips her fingers in and licks them, grinning.

Then she switches. Now she is Krishna's mother, Yashoda, hands on hips, eyebrows raised. A moment later she is Krishna again, eyes wide and innocent. The song may repeat the same line many times, and each time the dancer shows a new shade of meaning. Audiences who know the stories enjoy spotting each fresh idea.

For centuries, the dance was kept alive mainly by women called *devadasis*, who served in temples and danced at courts. In the early 1900s, reformers attacked the devadasi system, and temple dancing was later banned by law in the Madras Presidency.

Rukmini Devi Arundale learned the dance and helped rename and reshape it as Bharatanatyam. In 1936, she founded Kalakshetra in Chennai. Others, like the great hereditary dancer T. Balasaraswati, argued that the old traditions should be kept closer to their roots. Historians still discuss both sides today: one view says the revival saved the dance, another that it pushed out the families who had carried it.

sec.h: Bells, cymbals and a busy December
sec.t:
A Bharatanatyam dancer wears *salangai*, strings of small bells tied around the ankles. A leader called the *nattuvanar* keeps time with small cymbals and calls out rhythm [[syllable|syllables]], like "tha dhi thom nam". The dancer's feet answer, sound for sound.

Every December, [[@chennai|Chennai]] hosts a huge season of music and dance, with hundreds of concerts in a few weeks. Bharatanatyam is also one of the most popular dances among Indian-American children, many of whom train for years for their *arangetram*. It is one of eight [[@indian-classical-dance|classical dances]] recognised in India.

text: In Hindustani music, the classical music of north India, many [[raga|ragas]] have a time of day when they are traditionally performed. Raag Bhairav belongs to dawn, Raag Yaman to early evening and Raag Darbari to late night. Some ragas belong to a season instead. The Malhar family is linked with the [[monsoon|monsoon]].

A raga is more than a scale. It is a set of notes with rules about which to stress, which to skip and how to glide between them. Together these give it a mood. Musicians believe each mood suits a certain time, much as some songs just feel like mornings.
This is an artistic tradition passed down over centuries, not a law of science.

events.d: Serious and calm, for the early morning.
Warm and longing, for the hot afternoon.
Sweet and open, often one of the first ragas students learn.
Deep and grand, for late at night.

myth: Singing Raag Deepak can light lamps, and singing Malhar can make it rain.
These are old legends, mostly told about the singer Tansen. They are loved stories, not recorded events. Rain comes from monsoon winds carrying moisture from the ocean.

sec.t:
Traditional Indian timekeeping split the day and night into eight prahars, or watches, of about three hours each. Ragas came to be grouped by prahar. Morning ragas tend to sound calm and serious. Evening ragas often feel sweet and open, as lamps are lit. Midnight ragas can be deep and slow.

In the early 20th century, the musicologist Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande tried to explain the pattern using the notes themselves. He noticed that many ragas sung around sunrise and sunset use a flattened version of the second note, Re. These twilight ragas are called *sandhi prakash* ragas, ragas of the light where night and day meet. Not every raga fits his scheme, and musicians still argue about the exceptions.

Seasonal ragas work a little differently. Raag Malhar and its relatives, such as Miyan ki Malhar, are sung during the rainy months, when the sky is heavy and the air smells of wet earth. Some musicians perform them at any hour during the rains. In spring, ragas such as Basant and Bahar take their turn.

Legends grew around these ragas. Tansen is said to have lit lamps by singing Raag Deepak, and to have brought rain with Malhar. These are stories, retold for centuries, not events anyone recorded. Real [[@monsoon|monsoon]] rain comes from winds carrying moisture in from the ocean.

sec.h: Does anyone still follow the clock?
sec.t:
In concerts, many Hindustani musicians still choose ragas to suit the hour, and some refuse to sing a morning raga at night. Recordings, radio and streaming have loosened the rule, though. Great performers such as [[@ravi-shankar|Ravi Shankar]] recorded ragas that listeners could play at any time, anywhere in the world.

[[@carnatic-hindustani|Carnatic music]], the classical music of south India, links some ragas with times of day but follows them much less strictly. Scientists have begun testing whether ragas really shift people's moods, with mixed results so far. For many listeners, the timing is simply part of the pleasure. The right raga at the right hour can make an ordinary evening feel like an occasion.

text: A disability is a long-term condition that affects how a person sees, hears, moves, thinks or learns. The World Health Organization says about 1 in 6 people on Earth live with a significant disability.

Many disability campaigners point out something important. A person in a [[@accessibility-tech|wheelchair]] is disabled most by a building with only stairs. [[@blindness-tech|A blind student]] is held back most by a book that comes only in print. Remove the barrier, and much of the problem goes away.

So making the world fair means designing it for everyone from the start: ramps and lifts, captions and [[@sign-language|sign language]], [[@braille|Braille]] and screen readers, and [[@jobs-teacher|teachers who adapt lessons]].

Many disabilities can't be seen at all. Hearing loss, dyslexia, autism, long-term illness and some visual impairments are often invisible. Wheelchair users are only a small share of disabled people.

sec.t:
For a long time, disability was seen mainly as a medical problem, something wrong with a person that doctors should fix. Campaigners call this the medical model.

From the 1970s, disabled activists offered another view, the social model. It says people are disabled by barriers around them: steps, narrow doors, missing information and other people's attitudes. Both ideas are useful. Medicine can help a lot. But the social model reminds us that society can change, too.

Many fixes are simple. Yellow tactile paving on railway platforms, with raised bumps, warns blind travellers of the edge. Talking buttons in [[@elevators|lifts]] announce each floor. Captions on videos help [[@hearing-aids|deaf viewers]], and also anyone watching on a noisy bus.

In 2015, India launched the Accessible India Campaign to make government buildings, stations and websites easier to use. Many Indian [[@life-money-world|banknotes and coins]] have marks or sizes that help people who can't see well tell them apart.

India's 2016 law says disabled children have the right to study in ordinary schools with support, instead of being sent away. This is called inclusive education. It might mean a ramp to the science lab, a classmate who takes notes, extra time in exams or textbooks in large print.

In the USA, a 1975 law, now called IDEA, promised every disabled child a free public education suited to their needs. Before it, many disabled American children were kept out of school altogether.

Researchers have found that inclusive classrooms tend to help everyone. Children learn to work with people who are different from them, and teachers find new ways to explain things that help all their pupils.

Sport has shown what disabled athletes can do. In 1972, Murlikant Petkar, who was badly wounded as a soldier, won [[@sport-paralympians-india|India's first Paralympic gold]], in swimming. Shooter Avani Lekhara won gold at both the Tokyo and Paris [[@paralympics|Paralympics]].

Inclusion means disabled people take part in decisions, in schools, offices, films and government. The disability rights movement has a motto: "Nothing about us without us." It means no plan for disabled people should be made without asking them first.

text: In the Himalaya, many shepherd families move their flocks with the seasons. In summer they climb to high meadows above the forests, where melting snow leaves rich grass. In winter they walk back down to warmer foothills and plains. This back-and-forth journey is called transhumance.

The best-known groups include the Gaddis of Himachal Pradesh, the Bakarwals of Jammu and Kashmir, and the Changpas of Ladakh. A flock may hold hundreds of [[@goats-sheep|sheep and goats]]. The shepherds walk with them on foot, with dogs for protection and ponies or mules to carry tents, food and salt.

options.t: To follow fresh grass as the snow melts high up, then escape the winter cold
Because the animals get bored of one place
To sell wool in different towns each month

st.reveal: High meadows are buried in snow for much of the year, but in summer they burst with grass. In winter the shepherds bring the flocks down to warmer hills and plains where there is still something to eat. This seasonal back-and-forth is called transhumance.

Most follow the same routes their families have used for generations, with known stopping places, grazing rights and dates. Forest departments issue grazing permits, and shepherds time their moves to the melting snow.

sec.t:
A Gaddi shepherd's year might start in the scrubby foothills of the Shivaliks. From around February or March, the flock starts moving uphill. The animals graze as they go, covering about 7–8 km a day, roughly the length of a long city walk with plenty of snacking. Shepherds avoid roads where they can and follow river valleys and old bridle paths.

The full climb to alpine meadows can take around three months. Lambs are often born during the journey, and shepherds may carry newborns over rough ground in their arms or tucked in their coats.

Leopards, bears, wolves and, high up, [[@snow-leopard|snow leopards]] all hunt sheep and goats. The Gaddi dog, a big, shaggy guard dog, protects the flock at night. Many wear iron collars with spikes, so a big cat can't grab them by the throat.

Losses still happen. [[predator|Predators]], falls and sudden snow can take a share of a flock in a bad year. Shepherds count their animals often and know many of them individually. Before crossing a dangerous pass, some families still make offerings to local gods, asking for a safe journey for people and animals alike.

sec.h: The Changpas of the cold desert
sec.t:
In Ladakh's Changthang plateau, above 4,000 m, Changpa herders raise goats in one of the coldest inhabited places in India. Winter nights can drop far below -30°C. To survive, their goats grow a super-fine undercoat of wool. That fibre is pashmina, combed out by hand each spring and woven into famous shawls, as told in the story of [[@art-pashmina|pashmina]].

Changpa families move between fixed pastures several times a year, living in tents made of yak hair.

Moving flocks with the seasons is an ancient practice found across mountain lands, from the Alps to the Andes. In the American West, shepherds from the Basque region of Spain and France arrived in the late 1800s and herded sheep across Nevada, Idaho and California. The Navajo of the southwestern USA have kept sheep for centuries too.

Life on the move is getting harder. Roads, dams, new farms and forest rules have blocked some old routes. Weather is less predictable, and fewer young people want such a tough life. In some years flocks travel by truck for part of the way.

Still, Himalayan shepherds supply wool, meat and skills that the mountains need. Their journey follows the same [[rhythm|rhythm]] as many wild animals, which also move up and down the mountains with the seasons, as you can see in [[@animal-migration-land|animal migrations on land]].

text: The Sherpas are a people of the high Himalaya. Most live in the Solukhumbu district of Nepal, in the valleys around Mount Everest. Others live in Sikkim and Darjeeling in India, and in Tibet. They have their own language, related to Tibetan, and most follow Tibetan Buddhism.
The name means "people from the east". Their ancestors crossed from eastern Tibet into Nepal about 500 years ago, over high mountain passes, and settled on land few others wanted.
For the past century, the world has known Sherpas mainly as the climbers who make Everest [[expedition|expeditions]] possible. They fix ropes, carry loads, guide climbers and often save lives.

st.prompt: Sherpas cope with thin mountain air better than most people. How do their bodies do it?

options.t: Their bodies use oxygen more efficiently
They have much bigger lungs than everyone else
They have extra-thick blood full of red cells

st.reveal: Studies suggest Sherpas get more energy out of each breath of oxygen, and their blood flows well through tiny vessels. Surprisingly, they do not have especially thick blood. Very thick blood would be harder for the heart to pump.

The Sherpas are an ethnic group with their own language, culture and history. Many work in mountaineering, but many others are farmers, teachers, doctors and business owners. Some porters and guides on Everest belong to other groups entirely.

sec.t:
Sherpa villages, such as Namche Bazaar and Khumjung, sit between about 3,000 and 4,000 metres above the sea. For centuries, families grew potatoes and barley, kept yaks, and traded salt and wool across the passes with Tibet.

Buddhism is part of daily life. Prayer flags flap on bridges and passes. Stones carved with prayers line the paths, and people walk past them on the left. Tengboche Monastery, with Everest rising behind it, is one of the most important in the region.

High up, each breath carries less oxygen. At Everest's summit, about 8,849 metres, the air holds roughly a third of the oxygen at sea level. Most visitors get headaches and breathlessness at Base Camp. Some fall seriously ill.

Sherpas cope better. Scientists studying them have found that their bodies seem to use oxygen more efficiently, getting more energy from less. Blood flows well through their smallest vessels. Over thousands of years of high-mountain living, their ancestors developed [[gene|genes]] that help with [[@altitude|altitude]].

They still feel the cold and the thin air, and many still use bottled oxygen near the top. But it gives them an edge.

{{story:bar-headed-goose}}

sec.h: Tenzing Norgay and the first ascent
sec.t:
On 29 May 1953, Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa who lived in Darjeeling, and Edmund Hillary of New Zealand became the first people known to stand on top of [[@everest-first|Everest]]. Tenzing had already been on several Everest attempts, including one in 1952 when he climbed higher than anyone before.

Asked later who reached the top first, the two men gave the same answer for years: they got there together, as a team. Tenzing went on to train young climbers at the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute in Darjeeling, founded in 1954.

Today, Sherpas hold many of Everest's biggest records. Kami Rita Sherpa reached the summit for the 32nd time in May 2026, more than any other person. Lhakpa Sherpa, a woman who grew up in the Makalu region, reached the top for the 11th time on the same day in May 2026, the most for any woman.

Sherpa climbers have also set records for speed and for climbing without bottled oxygen. In 2021, a team of ten Nepali climbers, most of them Sherpas, became the first to climb K2, the world's second-highest mountain, in winter.

Mountain work pays far better than most jobs in the region, so many young Sherpa men take it on. But it is dangerous. Climbing guides cross the Khumbu Icefall many more times than their clients, carrying gear through a maze of moving ice. In April 2014, an avalanche there killed 16 Nepali mountain workers, most of them Sherpas.

After that disaster, many Sherpas demanded better pay, insurance and respect. Sherpa-owned companies now run many Everest expeditions themselves. Some families also send their children abroad to study, and the next generation may choose very different jobs.

High above their heads, a bird named the [[@bar-headed-goose|bar-headed goose]] flies over the Himalaya each year on migration, crossing passes at heights where most humans would struggle to stand.

text: Only three regular shapes tile a floor with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons. [[@circles|Circles]] leave spaces between them, and so do pentagons.

Of those three, hexagons enclose the most space for the length of their walls. Wax is precious. Bees eat a lot of honey to make it, several times more honey than the wax they produce. So the shape that holds the most honey for the least wall saves the colony a great deal of work.
Scientists think bees start with round-ish cells that get pulled into hexagons as the warm wax settles. Others think the bees shape the corners themselves.

st.prompt: Why do you think bees use hexagons?

st.reveal: Hexagons fit together with no gaps, like tiles, and they hold the most honey for the least wax. In 1999, mathematician Thomas Hales proved that no other way of dividing a flat space into equal cells uses less wall.
st.nudge: A fun idea! But the real reason is about saving wax.

sec.t:
Around 1,700 years ago, the Greek mathematician Pappus of Alexandria wrote that bees had a kind of "geometrical forethought". He argued that hexagons hold more than squares or triangles of the same wall length. Writers before him had made the same guess.

Proving it was much harder. Mathematicians had to show that no shape at all, even one with curved or wiggly sides, could beat the hexagon. In 1999, the American mathematician Thomas Hales finally did it. His proof covered every possible way of dividing a flat surface into equal areas. The bees had been right all along.

sec.h: Do bees build hexagons on purpose?
sec.t:
Here scientists disagree. In 2013, a team of engineers reported that bees first build round cells. Bees warm the wax with their bodies, and the soft walls flow and straighten where neighbouring cells meet, a bit like [[@bubbles-round|soap bubbles]] pushing against each other.

Other researchers watched bees closely and argued that the insects do much of the shaping themselves, measuring walls with their heads and legs. Both sides agree on one thing: the final shape is very close to a perfect hexagon.

You can test the idea with a simple sum. Take a shape with an area of 1 square centimetre. As a square, it needs walls 4 centimetres long all the way round. As a triangle, it needs about 4.6 centimetres. As a hexagon, it needs only about 3.7 centimetres.

That sounds like a small difference. But a single comb can hold thousands of cells, and a strong colony may build many combs. Across the whole hive, choosing hexagons saves a lot of wax, and a lot of the honey that bees would otherwise have to eat to make it.

In India, giant rock bees build single combs that can be more than a metre wide, hanging from cliffs, water tanks and even tall buildings. Up close, every cell is still a hexagon.

Engineers copy the shape too. The James Webb Space Telescope's main mirror is made of 18 gold-coated hexagons that fit together into one big mirror, as described in [[@webb-telescope|the Webb telescope]]. Hexagon floor tiles, football patterns and [[@tessellations|tessellations]] drawn by artists all borrow the same trick. A shape that wastes nothing turns out to be useful everywhere.

text: The World Series is the championship of Major League Baseball (MLB), the top professional baseball league in North America. Every October, the winner of the American League plays the winner of the National League. The first team to win four games takes the title.

The first modern World Series was played in 1903. Since then it has been held almost every year. It is one of the oldest championships in American sport, and baseball fans call it the "Fall Classic", because it happens in autumn.

st.reveal: In the 1880s, early championship games were already called the "World's Championship Series". American baseball was the top level of the sport, so the name felt natural. The newspaper story is a popular myth.

sec.t:
An MLB season is long. Each of the 30 teams plays 162 games from spring to the end of September. The best teams then enter the playoffs, a set of knockout rounds. Only two teams are left standing for the World Series.

The series is best of seven. The first two games are played at the home of the team with the better season, then two or three at the other team's park, then back again if needed. A best-of-seven reduces the role of luck. One bad day can lose a single match, but the stronger team usually wins four out of seven, which is a lesson in [[@probability|probability]].

Fans love stories of bad luck. In 1920 the Boston Red Sox sold their star, Babe Ruth, to the New York Yankees. The Yankees became the most successful team in baseball, with 27 titles. The Red Sox did not win again until 2004. Fans blamed "the Curse of the Bambino", after Ruth's nickname.

The [[@chicago|Chicago]] Cubs had an even longer wait. They won in 1908 and then not again until 2016, 108 years later. When they finally won, in a tense seventh game that went to extra innings, millions of people filled the streets of Chicago to celebrate.

sec.h: Is it really a world championship?
sec.t:
Only one team from outside the USA has ever won: the Toronto Blue Jays of Canada, in 1992 and 1993. But many players come from other countries, especially the Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Cuba, Japan and South Korea.

In 2024 the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the New York Yankees with help from Japanese stars like Shohei Ohtani, who both pitches and bats. Baseball is also huge in Japan, where crowds fill stadiums for the national high school [[tournament|tournament]].

Baseball and [[@cricket-history|cricket]] are distant cousins, both bat-and-ball games that grew from older English games. In both, a bowler or pitcher throws to a batter, and fielders try to catch the ball or get runners out.

The differences are big too. A baseball bat is round, and the ball can only be hit forwards into a wedge-shaped field. There are three strikes, not one wicket. Still, the World Series final innings can feel as tense as the last over of a World Cup final.

text: Cricket came to India with the British. Indians soon made it their own. It spread from army camps and clubs to schools, [[@princely-states|princely states]] and city streets, and after India won the World Cup in 1983, it became a national passion.
Gully cricket needs just a bat, a ball and some imagination. A wall can be the wicket, a rubber ball replaces the leather one, and every street has its own rules.
Today, India has more cricket fans than any other country. Its cricket board is the richest in the sport, and its stars are among the most famous people in the country.

sec.t:
In 1721, British sailors from an [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] ship played cricket near Khambhat, in Gujarat. A sailor named Clement Downing wrote about it in a book in 1737. It is the first recorded cricket in India.

For a long time, cricket was a game for British soldiers and officials. The Calcutta Cricket Club was founded in 1792. Then the Parsis of Bombay, a community of traders, took it up keenly. They formed clubs in the 1840s and toured England in 1886. Hindu, Muslim and other community teams followed.

India played its first Test match in 1932, at Lord's in London, led by C.K. Nayudu. It took 20 years and 25 Tests to win one, against England in Madras in 1952.

The big turning point came in 1983. India's men, led by Kapil Dev, were outsiders at the World Cup in England, but they beat the mighty West Indies in the final at Lord's. Colour TV had arrived in India the year before, and millions watched. Children everywhere started playing in streets and gullies.

India won the World Cup again in 2011, with the final in Mumbai, and the T20 World Cup in 2007, 2024 and 2026. In 2008, the Indian Premier League began, turning cricket into a TV show watched by crores.

Indian women have played [[@test-cricket|Test cricket]] since 1976. For years they got little money or attention. Stars like [[@mithali-raj|Mithali Raj]], who played international cricket for over 20 years, helped change that. In 2025, India's women won their first ODI World Cup, beating South Africa in the final in Navi Mumbai.

Cricket was once popular in the USA. The first international match ever played was between the USA and [[@canada|Canada]] in New York in 1844. Then baseball took over, and cricket faded.

Now it is returning. Many South Asian families in America play, the USA co-hosted the T20 World Cup in 2024, and cricket will be part of the [[@olympics|Olympics]] in [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]] in 2028. A game that left India's shores as a British habit is now being carried back across the world by Indian fans.

It shows two human figures spiralling upwards and holding up the Earth. The Italian sculptor Silvio Gazzaniga designed it, and it has been used since 1974. Winners only borrow it for the celebration, then FIFA takes it back and gives them a gold-plated copy.

sec.h: The first trophy and the dog
sec.t:
Before 1974, teams played for a different trophy, made of gold-plated silver and named after Jules Rimet, the Frenchman who started the World Cup. It was smaller, showing a winged figure of Victory.

In March 1966, a few months before England hosted the World Cup, the Jules Rimet Trophy was stolen from an exhibition in London. A week later, a black-and-white dog called Pickles was out for a walk with his owner in south London. He sniffed at a parcel wrapped in newspaper under a hedge. Inside was the trophy. Pickles became a national hero and even appeared in a film.

Brazil won the Jules Rimet Trophy for a third time in 1970 and was allowed to keep it for ever. In 1983, thieves broke into the Brazilian football federation's offices in Rio de Janeiro and stole it. It has never been found. Many people believe it was melted down for its gold.

That is one reason FIFA guards today's trophy so carefully. When it tours the world before each [[tournament|tournament]], it travels with security staff and is kept under glass.

Underneath the base, the names of the winning countries are engraved on a plate, starting with West Germany in 1974. There is room for winners up to 2038. After that, FIFA will have to change the plate or find another solution.

Argentina won in 2022, with [[@messi-ronaldo|Lionel Messi]] lifting the trophy in Qatar. The 2026 World Cup, played across the USA, Canada and Mexico, was the first with 48 teams. Spain beat Argentina 1–0 in the final in New Jersey, on 19 July 2026.

Malachite is a copper mineral with swirling bands of green, the colour of a football pitch. It has been polished into jewellery and decoration for thousands of years, and Russian palaces once used it for whole columns and tables. On the trophy, it is the only part that isn't gold.

India has never played at a men's World Cup, though it qualified in 1950 and did not go. Even so, millions of fans in Kolkata, Kerala and Goa, the country's football heartlands, stay up past midnight to watch the final. Few sporting prizes are guarded so closely. Its only real rivals for security are royal treasures such as the [[@crown-jewels|Crown Jewels]] in London, kept behind bombproof glass.

text: Skateboard tricks work by using the board as a [[lever|lever]] and the skater's feet to steer it through the air. In the basic trick, the ollie, the skater snaps the tail of the board down hard against the ground. The tail bounces up and the whole board pops into the air.

At the same moment, the skater jumps and slides the front foot forward along the rough grip tape on top. That drags the front of the board upwards until it is level. To the watcher, the board seems glued to the feet. Almost every other trick, from kickflips to grinds, starts with an ollie.

Air rushing under the board pushes it up

st.reveal: First the back foot snaps the tail down, so the board pops up. Then the front foot drags forward over the sandpaper-like grip tape, pulling the nose up and levelling the board.

If you simply jump, the board stays on the ground. The skater has to pop the tail and drag the board up with their front foot, using friction from the grip tape.

sec.t:
Skateboarding began in California in the 1950s, when [[@sport-surfing|surfers]] wanted something to do when the sea was flat. They fixed roller-skate wheels to planks of wood and called it sidewalk surfing. Its moves still borrow from riding [[@waves-how|waves]].

The first boards had clay or metal wheels that were noisy, slippery and dangerous on rough ground. Skateboarding faded in the 1960s, partly because so many riders got hurt.

The ollie was invented in 1978 by a Florida skater, Alan Gelfand, nicknamed "Ollie", on ramps. In 1982 Rodney Mullen worked out how to do it on flat ground. Street skating was born.

Here is the physics. The board works as a [[@lever-lift|lever]], with the back wheels as the pivot. Stamping on the tail pushes the board's front up and the tail down. When the tail strikes the ground, it rebounds and the board leaps. Then [[@friction|friction]] between shoe and grip tape lets the front foot drag the board up. Finally the skater pushes the front down to level it and bends the knees to land.

Once a skater can ollie, other tricks open up. In a kickflip, the front foot flicks off the edge of the board so it spins under the skater before they land. In a grind, the skater ollies onto a rail or ledge and slides along it on the metal trucks that hold the wheels.

Spins work like a [[@gymnastics|gymnast's]] somersault. Skaters crouch and pull their arms in to spin faster, then stretch out to slow down before landing. The best skaters can spin 900 or even 1,080 degrees, that is three full turns, above a ramp.

sec.h: From car parks to the Olympics
sec.t:
For years skateboarding was a street culture, and skaters were often chased out of plazas and car parks. Many cities now build skateparks instead. India has growing skate scenes too, in cities such as Bengaluru and in village skateparks built by community groups.

Skateboarding joined the [[@olympics|Olympics]] at the Tokyo Games, held in 2021, with street and park events. Several medallists were teenagers. Its basic tool still has just four [[@wheel-invented|wheels]], two axles and a board, and much of what a skater learns is how to fall safely, which is why [[@helmets|helmets]] and pads matter.

text: When your brain decides something is a threat, it switches on an alarm system. Within seconds, two small [[gland|glands]] sitting on top of your kidneys release [[adrenaline|adrenaline]] into your blood. Your heart beats faster and harder. You breathe more quickly. Your muscles tense, your palms sweat and your mouth goes dry. Your stomach may feel full of butterflies.

All of this gets your body ready to fight or to run. It's called the fight-or-flight response. For our ancestors, the threat might have been a leopard or a rival. For you, it might be an exam, a stage show or a first day at a new school. Your body reacts in much the same way, even though you don't need to run.

options.t: The body is moving blood and energy away from digestion towards the muscles

st.reveal: The alarm response puts eating and digesting on hold, because escaping comes first. Less saliva is made, and the stomach's blood supply drops, which feels like butterflies. It all goes back to normal once the moment passes.

myth: All stress is bad for you.
Short bursts of stress can help you focus and perform, such as before a match or a test. Problems come mainly when stress goes on for a long time without rest, or feels too big to handle alone.

sec.t:
The alarm starts in the [[@brain-works|brain]]. A part that watches for danger signals the hypothalamus, which acts like a control room. It sends messages down nerves to the adrenal glands, and adrenaline floods out.

Adrenaline makes your [[@heartbeat-exercise|heart]] pump more blood to your muscles. Your airways open wider to take in more oxygen. Your [[@liver|liver]] releases stored sugar for quick energy. Your pupils widen to let in more light. [[@stomach-digest|Digestion]] slows down, because there's no point digesting lunch while escaping a leopard. Blood moves away from the stomach, which is part of why it feels strange. A slower [[hormone|hormone]], cortisol, keeps the body's energy up if the threat lasts.

The alarm system is built for short emergencies. The trouble comes when it stays switched on for weeks, because of worries at home, at school or with friends. Then people may sleep badly, get headaches or tummy aches, feel tired, or catch colds more easily.

That doesn't mean something is wrong with you. It means your body is working hard and needs rest and support. Good [[@sleep-why|sleep]], exercise, time outdoors and time with people you trust all help bring the system back to calm. If worries feel too big or go on for a long time, telling a parent, teacher, school counsellor or doctor is a smart and brave step.

The body has a calming system too, which slows the heart and restarts [[digestion|digestion]]. One of the quickest ways to switch it on is to breathe slowly, making each breath out longer than the breath in. Breathing practices taught in yoga, found across India for many centuries, use the same idea.

Other things help as well: a walk, a good laugh, a hug, music or writing worries down on paper. The [[biologist|biologist]] Robert Sapolsky called one of his books Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers. A zebra's alarm switches off soon after the lion has gone, but people can keep theirs running for weeks just by worrying. With practice, people can learn to switch theirs off more like the zebra.

text: Indira Gandhi was the prime minister of India from 1966 to 1977, and again from 1980 until 1984. She was the country's first woman prime minister and is still the only one. She was also the daughter of [[@nehru|Jawaharlal Nehru]], India's first prime minister.

She was one of the most powerful leaders India has had. Supporters remember her for winning a war, helping India grow more of its own food and standing up to big countries. Critics remember her for the Emergency, when she suspended many of India's freedoms for nearly two years. Both memories are true, which is why she is still argued about.

sec.h: Growing up in the freedom struggle
sec.t:
Indira was born in 1917 in Allahabad, in a house that was a meeting place for leaders of the freedom movement. Her father and grandfather were often in prison. As a child she organised a Vanar Sena, a "monkey army" of children who carried messages and made flags.

She studied at Rabindranath Tagore's school in Santiniketan and later at Oxford. Her mother, Kamala, was often ill and died in Switzerland in 1936, when Indira was 18. After independence she lived with her father in Delhi and worked beside him, meeting world leaders long before she held any job of her own.

When Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri died suddenly in 1966, Congress party leaders chose Indira. Some of them thought she would be easy to control. They were wrong. Within a few years she had split the party and taken charge.

In 1969 her government took over 14 large private banks, so that farmers and small businesses could borrow more easily. She won the 1971 election with the slogan "Garibi hatao" (remove poverty). That same year India fought the [[@1971-war|1971 war]], which ended with the birth of Bangladesh. Her government also backed the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]], and in 1974 India tested its first nuclear device at Pokhran.

She was given the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, in 1971. In 1973 her government started Project Tiger, setting up nine special reserves to protect India's falling number of tigers. Abroad, she kept India out of both Cold War camps. In 1983 she hosted a summit in New Delhi of the Non-Aligned Movement, a large group of countries that refused to side with either the USA or the Soviet Union.

{{story:president-pm}}

In 1975 a court found her guilty of breaking election rules, and protests against her grew. On 25 June 1975 she declared a state of [[@emergency-1975|Emergency]]. Elections were put off. Thousands of opposition leaders were jailed without trial. Newspapers had to show their stories to government officers before printing. In some places, people were forced into operations to stop them having children.

She ended the Emergency in 1977 and called an election. Voters threw her out. It was the first time Congress had lost power at the centre since independence. Three years later, with the new government falling apart, voters brought her back.

In the early 1980s, armed separatists in Punjab took over buildings inside the Golden Temple in Amritsar. In June 1984 she ordered the army to remove them. Many people died, including soldiers and pilgrims, and the holy site was damaged. Many Sikhs felt deeply hurt.

On 31 October 1984 she was shot by two of her own bodyguards at her home in Delhi. Days of violence against Sikhs followed in Delhi and other cities, and thousands of innocent people were killed. Her son Rajiv Gandhi became prime minister. Her home is now a museum, where the path she walked that morning is marked with crystal.

text: Yes, more or less, though it wasn't a real war. In late 1932, farmers in Western Australia asked for help because around 20,000 emus were eating and trampling their wheat. The government sent a small team of soldiers with two machine guns.

The emus were faster, sharper and better at scattering than anyone expected. After weeks of chasing, the soldiers had used thousands of bullets and the farms were still full of emus. The army pulled out. Newspapers had a field day, and the strange campaign has been remembered as the "Emu War" ever since.

st.prompt: Why were the machine guns so poor at stopping the emus?

options.t: The emus wore armour-like feathers that stopped bullets

The soldiers refused to shoot

st.reveal: Emus can sprint at about 50 km/h and scatter at the first shot. Instead of a big flock to aim at, the soldiers faced dozens of small groups zigzagging away across the fields, and one of the guns jammed.

myth: Australia formally declared war on emus.
No war was ever declared. It was a pest-control job carried out with army soldiers and weapons. Newspapers called it the Emu War, and the name stuck.

sec.t:
After the First World War, Australia gave many returning soldiers land to farm. Plenty of them ended up in the dry wheat country of Western Australia. Then the [[@great-depression|Great Depression]] arrived in 1929, wheat prices crashed, and these farmers were already struggling.

Emus normally move towards the coast after breeding. The newly cleared farmland, with water tanks for livestock and fields of grain, was perfect for them. In 1932 a huge wave of the birds moved onto the farms around Campion. They ate crops and broke fences, which let rabbits in too.

The farmers, many of them former soldiers, asked the defence minister for machine guns. In November 1932, Major G. P. W. Meredith of the Royal Australian Artillery arrived with two soldiers, two Lewis guns and about 10,000 rounds of ammunition.

It went badly from the first day. Whenever the soldiers got close, the emus split into small groups and ran. One plan was to wait in ambush by a dam where a thousand emus gathered. The gun jammed after only a few birds had been hit. Someone tried mounting a gun on a truck, but the truck couldn't keep up on the rough ground and the gunner couldn't aim.

The operation was stopped after about a week, restarted at the farmers' request, and finally ended in December. Meredith claimed 986 emus killed using about 9,860 rounds, roughly 10 bullets per bird. Thousands more remained. The defence minister was even asked about it in Parliament, and some politicians wondered whether medals should go to the emus. Meredith himself is often quoted as saying, in admiration, that an army with the bullet-carrying toughness of emus could face any force in the world.

In the years after, the government offered farmers a small payment, called a bounty, for every emu they killed. Farmers knew their own land and could deal with birds steadily over months. Bounties removed far more emus than the soldiers ever had. Better fences also helped keep the birds off crops. Long barrier fences, some stretching hundreds of kilometres, were built across Western Australia to keep emus, rabbits and wild dogs away from farmland.

Emus are now protected in most of Australia, and the [[species|species]] is common. It appears on the country's coat of arms beside a kangaroo. Conflicts between farmers and wildlife still happen worldwide, much like the struggles with [[@invasive-species|invasive species]], though here it was the farms that were the newcomers.

text: The Oregon Trail was a long wagon route across the middle of North America. From the 1840s to the 1860s, families set off from towns on the Missouri River, such as Independence, and headed west to the green farmland of Oregon's Willamette Valley. The trip covered about 3,200 km (2,000 miles) of prairie, desert and mountains and took four to six months.

Roughly 300,000 to 400,000 people travelled the western trails in those years, including routes that branched off to California and Utah. They wanted free or cheap land, gold or a fresh start. For the [[@native-nations|Native nations]] already living along the way, the flood of wagons brought disease and the loss of land.

st.reveal: Cholera, spread by dirty water at crowded campsites, killed far more people than anything else. Accidents, such as falling under wagon wheels or drowning at river crossings, came next. Fighting with Native Americans caused only a small share of deaths.

sec.t:
Travellers measured progress by famous rocks. Chimney Rock, a tall spire in Nebraska, could be seen for days. At Independence Rock in Wyoming, they hoped to arrive by 4 July, to be sure of crossing the mountains before snow fell. Thousands carved their names into it.

At Guernsey, Wyoming, wagon wheels wore ruts up to about 1.5 m deep into soft sandstone. You can still walk in them today. In other places, faint wagon tracks across grassland are visible from the air more than 150 years later.

The trail's worst danger was invisible. Cholera, a disease spread by dirty water, swept through crowded campsites. A person could feel fine at breakfast and be dead by evening. Historians estimate that somewhere between one in twenty and one in ten travellers died on the journey, though numbers are uncertain.

River crossings were scary too, because wagons could tip and people drown. Then came the mountains. Families had to haul wagons over the [[@rocky-mountains|Rocky Mountains]] and the Blue Mountains, sometimes lowering them down cliffs with ropes. Precious furniture was dumped along the way to lighten the load.

sec.h: The other side of the story
sec.t:
The trail cut through land that had belonged to Native nations for thousands of years, including the Lakota, Cheyenne, Shoshone and many others. At first, many tribes traded horses, salmon and help with river crossings. As tens of thousands of wagons passed each year, though, settlers' animals ate the grass and hunters killed bison. New diseases spread.

The US government used the trail to strengthen its claim to Oregon, which Britain also wanted. Settlement led to [[treaty|treaties]], wars and the forced removal of Native peoples onto reservations.

The trail's busy years ended when the [[@transcontinental-railroad|transcontinental railroad]] opened in 1869. A trip of months shrank to about a week. People still used parts of the route afterwards, but the great wagon trains faded into history.

They came back to life in an unexpected way. In 1971, three student teachers in Minnesota made a computer game called The Oregon Trail. Players chose supplies, hunted for food and tried not to "die of dysentery". It became one of the most played educational games ever, and a chapter in the [[@video-game-history|history of video games]].

text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a giant freezer dug into a mountain on Spitsbergen, an island in Norway's Svalbard islands, far north in the [[@arctic|Arctic]] Ocean. Inside are seeds of rice, wheat, beans, millets and thousands of other crops from almost every country.

It isn't meant to be used every day. It is a backup. Countries keep their own seed banks, but those can be hit by floods, fires, wars or broken freezers. If that happens, a spare copy is waiting in Svalbard. By the end of 2025, it held about 13.7 lakh seed samples from 131 depositors.

st.reveal: The vault works like a bank's safe deposit box. Norway looks after the building, but each box of seeds still belongs to whoever deposited it, and only they can take it out.

myth: It is against the law to die in Svalbard.
There is no such law. But bodies buried in the frozen ground do not decay, so burials in Longyearbyen stopped long ago, and people who are very ill or old are usually flown to mainland Norway.

sec.t:
Svalbard is about 1,300 km from the North Pole. The ground stays frozen all year, a layer called [[permafrost|permafrost]]. Even if the electricity failed, the rock around the vault would stay well below freezing for a long time.

The vault sits about 130 m above sea level, high enough to stay dry even if all the ice on Earth melted. It is also far from wars and big cities. Norway runs it for free, together with the Crop Trust and a Nordic [[gene|gene]] bank called NordGen.

From outside, all you see is a narrow concrete wedge sticking out of the snow. At night its top glows with an artwork of mirrors and lights. Behind the door, a tunnel runs more than 100 m into the rock.

At the end are three halls, kept at minus 18 °C. Seeds are sealed in foil packets, packed in plain boxes and stacked on shelves like books in a library. Each sample usually holds about 500 seeds. At this cold, many seeds can stay alive for decades or centuries.

Scientists have even started an experiment to find out exactly how long. In 2008 they sealed packets of 13 crops in the vault, planning to test a few every five years, for a hundred years. The last packets will be opened in 2108. Some seeds, like sorghum and pea, may last for thousands of years at this cold.

{{story:green-revolution}}

For years, a research centre in Aleppo, Syria, held a huge collection of wheat, barley and lentil seeds adapted to dry lands. When war broke out there, scientists couldn't keep it running. In 2015, they asked for their backup copies from Svalbard.

The seeds were sent to new gene banks in Lebanon and Morocco, planted, and grown into fresh seed. Some were later sent back to the vault. It was the first time anyone had needed it, and it worked as planned.

India's gene banks and research centres also send seeds. ICRISAT, a crop research institute near Hyderabad, has deposited samples of chickpea, sorghum, pigeon pea and [[@millets|millets]], crops that feed millions of people in dry regions. India also runs a research station called Himadri in Svalbard, where its scientists study Arctic weather and [[glacier|glaciers]].

Many of these seeds come from old local varieties that farmers grew for generations. Some may hold the secret to surviving heat, [[drought|drought]] or new diseases.

The nearest town, Longyearbyen, has around 2,500 people, a school, a university centre and a supermarket. Polar bears live on the islands, so anyone leaving town is advised to carry protection and travel with a guide. From late October to mid-February the sun never rises.

Svalbard is also unusual politically. Under a [[treaty|treaty]] from 1920, it belongs to Norway, but citizens of the countries that signed it can live and work there without a visa. That is why Russian miners, Thai cooks and Indian scientists can all be found on the same Arctic islands.

In 2017, unusually warm weather sent meltwater into the entrance tunnel. No seeds were harmed, but the tunnel was rebuilt. It was a small sign of how [[@climate-change|climate change]] is warming the Arctic faster than almost anywhere else.

text: A book fair is a giant market for books. Publishers and booksellers set up stalls, sometimes hundreds or thousands of them, and visitors wander between them, flicking through new titles and old favourites. Authors give talks and sign copies. There are often children's corners, quizzes, music and plenty of food.

There are two main kinds. At trade fairs, like the one in Frankfurt, publishers mostly do business with each other, buying and selling the rights to print books in other countries. At public fairs, like the ones in Kolkata and New Delhi, the main visitors are readers, families and school groups who come to buy and browse.

sec.t:
Soon after Johannes Gutenberg began printing with movable type in Mainz in the 1450s, printers began taking their books to the trade fairs in nearby Frankfurt. Booksellers came from all over Europe to buy them. The [[@printing-press|printing press]] had made books cheaper, and Frankfurt became the place to sell them.

Today's Frankfurt Book Fair was restarted in 1949, after the Second World War. Each October, thousands of publishers from more than 100 countries meet there. The main business is rights. A deal made over coffee in Frankfurt can mean a Hindi novel being read in Spanish a year later, thanks to [[@translation|translation]].

sec.h: The New Delhi World Book Fair
sec.t:
India's other giant fair, the New Delhi World Book Fair, has been organised by the National Book Trust since 1972. It is held at the exhibition grounds at Pragati Maidan in [[@delhi|Delhi]], now home to a new convention centre called Bharat Mandapam. Publishers come from India and abroad, and books are sold in English, Hindi, Urdu, Tamil, Bengali and many other languages.

School groups arrive by the busload. Children's halls are packed with comics, picture books and science kits, and storytellers perform for small crowds sitting on the floor.

In the USA, many children meet their first book fair in the school library. Scholastic, a children's publisher, has run book fairs in American schools since 1981. Cases on wheels are unfolded into shelves, and children browse during class time with a little money from home. Many adults remember the smell of new books and the shiny posters and pencils sold alongside them.

Italy hosts the Bologna Children's Book Fair, started in 1964, where illustrators and children's publishers from around the world trade ideas and rights. A picture book drawn in Bengaluru may find a publisher in Brazil there.

Online shops can deliver almost any book. But fairs let you discover books you would never have searched for. Small publishers, poets and translators get a stall next to the big names. And for many families, a day at the fair, with a full bag of books and a plate of snacks at the end, is a tradition that has lasted generations.

text: People called [[lexicographer|lexicographers]] decide what goes into a dictionary, but they don't decide which words are allowed. Their job is to watch the language. They collect millions of examples of words in books, [[@newspapers|newspapers]], websites, song lyrics and transcripts of speech. They add a word when it is used widely, by many different people, over a period of time.

So, in a way, you help decide. If enough people use a new word for long enough, it will probably end up in the dictionary. Words that drop out of use stay in big dictionaries too, marked "old" or "archaic", so that readers of older books can still look them up.

Every word starts out of the dictionary. Lexicographers add words after people have used them for a while, so plenty of real words are simply too new, too local or too rare to be included yet.

sec.t:
People have made word lists for thousands of years. Scribes in ancient [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] made clay tablets listing words in Sumerian alongside their meanings in Akkadian. In India, the *Amarakosha*, a [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] word book written in verse more than a thousand years ago, grouped words by meaning: words for gods, plants, animals, people and much more. Students memorised it by chanting.

The first English dictionaries, in the early 1600s, mostly explained "hard words", difficult terms borrowed from [[@latin-roots|Latin]] or French. They left out everyday words like "dog" or "bread", on the grounds that everyone knew them already.

In 1755, Samuel Johnson published *A Dictionary of the English Language*. With a handful of helpers, he spent about nine years defining some 42,000 words and backing them with quotations from famous writers. Some definitions were cheeky. He described a lexicographer as "a harmless drudge", someone doing dull, hard work.

In the USA, Noah Webster wanted [[@english-spread|American English]] to have its own identity. His *American Dictionary of the English Language*, published in 1828, dropped the u from *colour* and *honour* and changed *centre* to *center*. That's one big reason American and British [[@words-spelling-bee|spellings]] differ, and why this app changes colour to color for readers in the USA.

sec.t:
Today, lexicographers use computers to search huge collections of text, called corpora, holding billions of words. When a new word appears, they ask: is it used by lots of different people, in different places, over several years? Or is it a flash in the pan?

[[@words-made-up|New words]] arrive all the time from technology, science and [[@slang|slang]]. "Selfie" was chosen as Oxford's [[@words-emoji-language|Word of the Year]] in 2013. Indian English adds words too: *jugaad*, a clever, low-cost fix, joined the Oxford English Dictionary in 2017. Online dictionaries now update every few months.

A [[@search-engines|search engine]] can show you a word's meaning in less than a second. Behind that answer is a team of people who read the evidence, argued over it and wrote the definition with care.
